explanation_text: On a Chinese abacus (suanpan), each column holds a place: the rightmost column counts ones, the next counts tens, and so on. Moving a bead one column left multiplies its value by ten, exactly as a digit's place changes its value. Reading a number off the abacus means reading the value of each column together.
image_prompt: A Chinese abacus with beads pushed toward the middle beam, columns labeled ones, tens, and hundreds, showing how position sets each bead's value.

explanation_text: At a Cantonese dim sum house, bamboo steamer baskets are stacked on a cart, and the stack grows as more dishes are added. Lifting baskets off to serve shrinks the stack. Adding to the stack increases the total count, and removing baskets decreases it, just like addition and subtraction.
image_prompt: A dim sum cart with bamboo steamer baskets being added to and lifted off a tall stack, with plus and minus symbols beside it.

explanation_text: Dumplings are arranged on a tray in neat rows of ten, so counting them by rows is repeated addition, which is multiplication. When the tray is shared so each person gets an equal number, the rows are split evenly, which is division.
image_prompt: A round tray with rows of pleated jiaozi dumplings, arrows showing groups being counted and then split into equal shares.

explanation_text: In northern homes, dumplings are traditionally served in even numbers so every person gets complete pairs. A plate holding ten dumplings pairs perfectly, making ten even. Leave one dumpling on the plate and that single leftover makes it odd.
image_prompt: A plate of dumplings arranged in matching pairs with one lone dumpling set aside, labeled even and odd.

explanation_text: Yangge dancers on northern streets move in repeated four-beat patterns, crossing the square step by step. Counting every fourth beat lands on 4, 8, 12, 16, the same rhythm as skip counting. The repeating dance phrase and the repeating number pattern share the same structure.
image_prompt: Village Yangge dancers with fans on a festive street, a sequence of steps marked 4, 8, 12, 16 to show skip counting.

chinese_culture: Sugar cane stalks of many lengths
explanation_text: At a southern market, a buyer holds sugar cane stalks side by side to see which is longer and which is shorter. Seeing which stalk is greater than another is comparing two quantities. Writing 8 > 5 or 5 < 8 records that comparison in number language.
image_prompt: Sugar cane stalks of different lengths laid side by side at a market stall, with a greater-than symbol between two of them.

explanation_text: When a vendor brews sweet-sour plum drink for a market day, the exact number of cups is hard to predict, so the batch is rounded to a convenient pot size. This is estimation, using a close, convenient number instead of a precise one. Rounding to the nearest full pot makes the plan practical.
image_prompt: A northern street vendor ladling suanmeitang into cups from large pots, with amounts labeled and rounded to the nearest pot.

chinese_culture: Sharing a basket of four buns
explanation_text: A dim sum basket holds four identical buns. If four people share it, each person takes one of the four equal parts, one quarter of the basket. A fraction names that equal share of a whole.
image_prompt: A bamboo steamer with four buns, one bun highlighted and labeled one-fourth, with the whole basket labeled one whole.

explanation_text: A cook cuts a wheat flatbread into two equal halves, then cuts each half into quarters. Two quarters of the bread and one half of the bread are the same amount of bread. Different fractions can name the same quantity, so they are equivalent.
image_prompt: A round northern flatbread cut first into halves then quarters, with the halves and quarters shown side by side as equal amounts.

explanation_text: If six of eight filled steamer baskets are ready to serve, six-eighths are done. Since both six and eight divide evenly by two, that is the same as three-quarters. Rewriting six-eighths as three-quarters is simplifying a fraction.
image_prompt: Eight bamboo steamer baskets with six labeled ready and two waiting, six-eighths shown equal to three-quarters.

explanation_text: A clay pot of fragrant rice with sausage fills two whole bowls and leaves a half bowl at the bottom. That amount is written 2 1/2, a whole part and a fraction part together. This combination is called a mixed number.
image_prompt: A clay pot rice dish with two full bowls and one half-full bowl, labeled 2 and 1/2 forming 2 1/2.

explanation_text: A hearty bowl of hand-pulled noodles might overflow one standard serving and fill a second bowl partway. Measured in standard servings, the amount is more than one whole serving. A fraction whose numerator is larger than its denominator is an improper fraction.
image_prompt: Hand-pulled lamian noodles spilling from one bowl into a second, labeled as five-fourths of a serving.

chinese_culture: Filling a pot with small tea cups
explanation_text: In a gongfu tea session, each small cup of tea is a fraction of the full teapot. Poured one after another into a larger vessel, the cups combine into a whole. Adding fractional amounts to build a total is how fractions are added.
image_prompt: A gongfu tea tray where small cups are emptied into a larger teapot, each cup labeled as a fraction of the whole.

explanation_text: A cook serves congee by ladling out portions from a full pot. When one quarter is served, three quarters remain. Taking a fractional part away and finding what is left is fraction subtraction.
image_prompt: A pot of congee with one serving being ladled out, the remaining amount labeled three-fourths.

explanation_text: A guest takes half of a bowl of wontons, and the chef gives them half of that serving, half of a half. Half of one half is one quarter of the whole bowl. Finding a part of a part is multiplying fractions.
image_prompt: A bowl of wontons divided in half, with one half divided again, the quarter portion highlighted.

explanation_text: A vendor stacks jianbing crepes and asks how many half-crepes make one whole crepe, and the answer is two. Asking how many of a smaller piece fit into a larger one is division with fractions.
image_prompt: A stack of folded jianbing crepes, one crepe cut in half with two halves shown fitting back into the whole.

explanation_text: A cook measures water for rice on a marked pot and stops at one and a half liters. The mark between one and two liters shows a tenth of the unit, making decimals visible. One and five tenths is written 1.5.
image_prompt: A clear pot with water beside a rice basin, a scale marked 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 liters.

chinese_culture: Legendary room count of the Forbidden City
explanation_text: Legend says the Forbidden City contains nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine and a half rooms, a number just shy of ten thousand. The half room means the same as 0.5 rooms, so nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine and one half and 9,999.5 describe the identical count. Writing the same quantity as a fraction or a decimal is conversion.
image_prompt: A bird's-eye view of the Forbidden City's halls, with the label 9999 1/2 shown equal to 9999.5.

explanation_text: At a lantern festival riddle contest, solving 85 of 100 riddles means earning 85 out of every hundred, which is 85 percent. Percent simply means out of one hundred. The riddle score converts into a per-hundred rate.
image_prompt: Festive paper lanterns with riddle slips, a scoreboard reading 85 out of 100 equals 85 percent.

explanation_text: A jianbing stall offers fifteen percent off an eight-yuan crepe. Finding fifteen percent of eight means taking fifteen out of every hundred of the price. This computes the actual amount of the discount.
image_prompt: A Beijing street jianbing stall with a sign reading 15 percent off, a crepe price tag showing the discounted yuan amount.

chinese_culture: Unlabeled baskets at the fish market
explanation_text: In a Guangzhou wet market, an unlabeled basket sits with the other fish baskets because no one has counted its catch yet. That unknown count can stand for a letter in math. A symbol that holds an unknown number is a variable.
image_prompt: A wet market stall with labeled fish baskets and one unlabeled basket marked x.

explanation_text: If three fish baskets are known to hold fish and one unlabeled basket holds an unknown number, the total is written 3 + x. Combining known numbers with a variable like this builds an algebraic expression. Expressions describe amounts before they are computed.
image_prompt: Four fish baskets at a market, three with fish counts and one marked x, joined by a plus sign as 3 + x.

explanation_text: A water carrier's bamboo shoulder pole balances only when the load on each end is equal. The two ends holding equal weight show the meaning of the equals sign. When both sides match, the situation reads like an equation.
image_prompt: A bamboo shoulder pole with two pails of water hanging in perfect balance, both ends labeled equal.

chinese_culture: A dumpling order on a tray
explanation_text: A customer orders ten dumplings and three are already on the tray, so the cook must add the missing seven. To find the missing number, take the three away from the ten. One single operation finds the unknown, a one-step equation.
image_prompt: A tray of dumplings with three placed and a blank space, labeled x plus 3 equals 10.

explanation_text: A buyer takes two tins of tea of the same price and adds a fixed gift-box fee, and the clerk writes the final total. Undoing the total requires two steps: subtract the gift-box fee, then divide by two. This mirrors solving a two-step equation.
image_prompt: A tea shop counter with two tins of tea and a wrapped gift box, the bill written as 2x plus 5 equals 21.

explanation_text: On the Pearl River, one sampan carries more rice baskets than another. The two loads are not equal, so their comparison is an inequality. The heavier load is greater than the lighter one, written with a greater-than sign.
image_prompt: Two sampans on the Pearl River, one stacked higher with cargo, a greater-than symbol between them.

chinese_culture: Clay pot rice cooked in order
explanation_text: Cooking clay pot rice follows a strict sequence: rinse the rice, measure the water, simmer, then add the sausages at the end. Reversing the steps ruins the dish. When an expression mixes operations, the order of doing them matters just as much.
image_prompt: A step-by-step diagram of clay pot rice: washing rice, simmering, then adding toppings, numbered like an ordered calculation.

explanation_text: A worn brick in a courtyard wall is replaced with an identical new brick, so the wall keeps its strength. In algebra, replacing a variable with its known value is substitution. The wall works the same whether its brick is named by the old piece or the new one.
image_prompt: A siheyuan courtyard wall with one brick being replaced by an identical one, the brick marked with the letter x equaling its value.

explanation_text: Visitors mark the Ten Scenes of West Lake on a map, each landmark becoming a single dot at its location. A dot that names an exact place is a point in geometry. Points mark positions without length or width.
image_prompt: A painted map of West Lake with ten dots at scenic spots, each dot labeled as a point.

explanation_text: Viewed from Jinshanling, the Great Wall runs along mountain ridgelines, and each long straight section stretches without bending. A geometric line is the same idea, a straight path that continues in both directions. The wall's straight stretches show lines in the landscape.
image_prompt: The Great Wall snaking along straight mountain ridges at Jinshanling, straight guide lines drawn over each section.

explanation_text: Where two hutong streets meet, the corner spreads open like the hands of a clock. The amount of turn at that corner is an angle, measured in degrees. A narrow lane junction forms a small angle and a wide crossing a large one.
image_prompt: A Beijing hutong intersection with a protractor drawn over the street corner, the angle measured in degrees.

explanation_text: In a siheyuan courtyard house, horizontal roof beams meet vertical columns squarely. Where they meet, the beams form right angles, and lines meeting at right angles are perpendicular. The square joints keep the courtyard structure firm.
image_prompt: A cutaway of a siheyuan house showing a beam meeting a column at a right angle, ninety-degree marks drawn at each joint.

explanation_text: The stepped rice terraces of Longji follow the hillside in long, curving rows that never cross one another. Each terrace edge runs side by side with the next at a steady spacing. Lines that stay the same distance apart and never meet are parallel.
image_prompt: The Longji rice terraces curving down a mountainside, with drawn parallel contour lines tracing each terrace edge.

explanation_text: Seen from above, each courtyard compound of the Forbidden City is a walled shape made of straight sides that close back on themselves. A closed, many-sided figure is a polygon. The rectangular compounds of the palace are polygons on a grand scale.
image_prompt: An aerial view of the Forbidden City's rectangular courtyard compounds, outlines traced to show closed polygons.

explanation_text: The gabled roofs of northern courtyard houses rise to a ridge, and the end wall beneath it forms a three-sided shape. The ridge, eave, and wall make a triangle. Because triangles hold their shape, they frame the gable without bending.
image_prompt: Rows of northern courtyard houses with gabled roofs, one triangular gable highlighted with its three sides.

explanation_text: Though round tulou are famous, many Hakka villages in Fujian built square earth houses whose walls form four straight sides. A four-sided closed shape is a quadrilateral. The square tulou's plan shows the quadrilateral in the layout of a home.
image_prompt: A square Hakka tulou earth house seen from above, its four walls traced to show a quadrilateral outline.

explanation_text: Visitors can walk the complete circuit of Pingyao's ancient rectangular walls. The full distance around the walls is the perimeter. Adding the lengths of all four sides gives the total distance of the walk.
image_prompt: Tourists walking along Pingyao's ancient city wall, a dashed line tracing the full rectangular circuit around the town.

explanation_text: A farmer measures how much of the Longji hillside a terrace covers. The flat surface the terrace spans is its area. Larger terraces hold more rice because they cover more area on the slope.
image_prompt: A single rice terrace on the Longji hillside shaded to show its surface area, with a grid of square measures drawn on it.

explanation_text: A porcelain teapot from Jingdezhen is judged partly by how much tea it can hold. The space inside a three-dimensional shape is its volume. Pouring tea until the pot is full measures that capacity.
image_prompt: A white-and-blue Jingdezhen porcelain teapot being filled with tea, its interior space labeled as volume.

explanation_text: The great round tulou of Fujian are built as exact circles so every family's room faces the shared courtyard. A line through the center from one wall to the other is the diameter, and half of that is the radius. The circular ring of rooms traces the circumference.
image_prompt: A round Hakka tulou seen from above, with radius and diameter lines drawn across the circular courtyard.

explanation_text: A round Cantonese mooncake always keeps the same relationship between its rim and its width. No matter the mooncake's size, the distance around divided by the distance across stays about 3.14. That constant ratio is the number pi.
image_prompt: Round Cantonese mooncakes of two sizes, each with circumference and diameter labeled, both ratios equal to 3.14.

explanation_text: Beijing's streets were laid out on a grid, with avenues running east-west and north-south crossing like the axes of a graph. Any intersection can be found by naming its street in each direction. Two crossing number lines like this form a coordinate plane.
image_prompt: An old map of Beijing's grid of straight streets with east-west and north-south axes drawn like graph lines.

explanation_text: Race officials mark each dragon boat's position on a chart as the race progresses down the river. Each mark names a boat's location with a pair of numbers. Placing a dot at its coordinates is plotting a point.
image_prompt: A dragon boat race chart with numbered lanes, dots marking each boat's position along the course.

explanation_text: Northern paper-cut artists fold a sheet of red paper in half, cut a design, and unfold it to reveal two identical halves. Each half mirrors the other across the fold. This mirror balance is symmetry, and the fold line is the mirror line.
image_prompt: A northern paper cutter folding red paper and cutting, the unfolded window decoration showing mirrored halves across the fold line.

explanation_text: In a Suzhou garden, pavilions and bridges reflect in the pond, and each reflection flips the structure across the waterline. Flipping a figure across a line is a reflection, one kind of geometric transformation. The garden pairs every building with its mirror image.
image_prompt: A Suzhou garden pavilion reflected in a calm pond, the waterline drawn as the mirror line of the reflection.

explanation_text: A gongfu tea master measures leaves against water in a fixed proportion, such as one part tea leaves to twenty parts water. Comparing two quantities with this fixed relationship is a ratio. Changing the ratio changes the strength of every cup.
image_prompt: A gongfu tea setup with a scoop of leaves and a kettle of water, the proportion written as one to twenty.

explanation_text: To copy a small paper-cut design as a large banner, the artist multiplies every measurement by the same factor. Each part of the design grows by the same amount, keeping the shapes faithful. Two ratios that stay equal while scaling are proportions.
image_prompt: A small paper-cut stencil beside a larger version of the same pattern, arrows showing every measurement scaled by the same factor.

explanation_text: A lamian chef can pull and serve a set number of noodle bowls every hour. The amount produced in one hour is a unit rate, written as bowls per hour. Comparing chefs' speed means comparing their unit rates.
image_prompt: A lamian chef pulling noodle dough, a counter showing bowls served per hour as the unit rate.

explanation_text: Cartographers draw Pingyao's walled town as a smaller plan, shrinking every street by the same fraction. Each centimeter on the plan stands for a fixed number of meters on the ground. A drawing that keeps real distances proportional is a scale drawing.
image_prompt: The walled town of Pingyao beside its map, a scale bar linking centimeters to meters.

explanation_text: An orchard's lychee harvest rises from two hundred to two hundred sixty baskets. The increase of sixty baskets is thirty percent of the original harvest. Comparing the change to the starting amount gives the percent change.
image_prompt: Southern lychee trees with baskets of fruit, a chart showing harvest rising from 200 to 260 baskets labeled 30 percent.

explanation_text: An orchard keeper walks the rows and records how many lychees each tree bears, writing the count on a tablet. Gathering numbers from the real world in an organized way is data collection. The recorded list becomes the raw material for charts and averages.
image_prompt: An orchard keeper counting lychees on a tree and writing tallies on a wooden tablet, baskets of fruit nearby.

explanation_text: Farmers on the North China Plain record each field's wheat harvest in rows and columns. The tidy rows and columns make the numbers easy to compare at a glance. Organizing data into a table is the first step before drawing graphs.
image_prompt: A wooden table ledger with wheat harvest numbers written in rows and columns beside golden wheat fields.

explanation_text: To describe a village's wheat harvest, farmers add the yield of every field and divide by the number of fields. The result is the mean, or average, yield per field. One number then represents the whole harvest fairly.
image_prompt: Wheat fields of differing sizes on the North China Plain, with the total harvest divided evenly and labeled as the mean per field.

explanation_text: Line up the year's wheat harvests from smallest to largest and the harvest in the exact middle is the median. The median is not swayed by one enormous field. It describes the center of the data in a stable way.
image_prompt: A row of harvest sacks lined up from shortest to tallest, the middle sack highlighted and labeled the median.

explanation_text: At a hutong's lantern festival street, red lanterns outnumber every other color. The value that appears most often in a set of data is the mode. Red is the mode of the lantern colors.
image_prompt: Lanterns in red, gold, and pink strung across a hutong lane, red shown as the most common color, labeled the mode.

explanation_text: On the Pearl River, the heaviest sampan carries twenty baskets and the lightest carries eight. Subtracting the smallest from the largest gives twelve, the spread of the data. The gap between the highest and lowest values is the range.
image_prompt: Sampans along a river carrying different numbers of cargo baskets, the heaviest and lightest marked to show the range.

explanation_text: To compare festival decorations, neighbors count the lanterns hanging on each hutong lane and draw one bar per lane. The tallest bar shows which lane has the most lanterns. Bars of different heights make comparison immediate.
image_prompt: A bar graph with one bar for each hutong lane showing lantern counts, the tallest bar highlighted.

explanation_text: A drink stall records suanmeitang sales each week through the hot months and joins the weekly totals with a line. The rising and falling line shows the trend of the season. Connecting data points reveals change over time.
image_prompt: A graph of suanmeitang cups sold across summer weeks, a rising and falling line connecting the weekly points.

explanation_text: A mahjong set holds tiles of three suits, and the whole set can be divided into its suit groups. A pie chart shows the proportion of each suit as a slice of the circle. The full circle is the whole set, and each slice is one part of it.
image_prompt: A mahjong set arranged by suits, with a pie chart beside it showing the share of each suit as colored slices.

explanation_text: Before a player draws, some tiles remain in the wall, and the chance of pulling a particular tile depends on how many of that tile are left. That chance is probability. Comparing the favorable tiles to all remaining tiles gives the odds.
image_prompt: A mahjong wall of face-down tiles with one hand drawing a tile, favorable tiles counted against all remaining tiles.

explanation_text: Wooden window lattices in northern courtyard houses repeat the same carved shape again and again across the frame. The shape that repeats in a fixed order is a pattern. Predicting the next cell means following the same rule.
image_prompt: A carved wooden window lattice repeating the same shape across a siheyuan window, the repeating unit highlighted.

explanation_text: In a dragon boat, every stroke rate gives the boat a matching speed through the water. For each input number of strokes, there is exactly one output speed. A rule that pairs each input with one output is a function.
image_prompt: A dragon boat race with a chart linking strokes per minute on one side to boat speed on the other.
